evidence.quote: Chytridiomycosis, an infectious disease of amphibians, has been reported in common toads in Spain and the United Kingdom and may affect some populations.

evidence.value: mue excessive, épaississement de la peau
evidence.quote: Excessive shedding of skin is seen in most frog species affected by B. dendrobatidis.
evidence.note: page générale sur les amphibiens, pas spécifique au crapaud commun

evidence.quote: The most typical symptom of chytridiomycosis is thickening of skin, which promptly leads to the death of the infected individuals.
Individuals infected are also commonly found in a lethargic state, characterized by slow movements, and refuse to move when stimulated.

evidence.value: rougeur, convulsions, perte du réflexe de redressement
evidence.quote: Other common signs are reddening of the skin, convulsions, and a loss of righting reflex.
Treatment is not always 100% successful and not all amphibians tolerate treatment very well, therefore chytridiomycosis should always be treated with the advice of a veterinarian.
The fly lays its eggs on the toad's skin, and when they hatch, the larvae crawl into the toad's nostrils and eat its flesh from inside, with lethal consequences.
Juveniles are often parasitised by the lung nematode Rhabdias bufonis. This slows growth rates and reduces stamina and fitness.
Their parasite-induced anorexia caused a decrease in food intake and some died.
